extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in the Penn State/Jerry Sandusky scandal
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style, chronological and referenced account of the Penn State/Jerry Sandusky child-sex-abuse scandal, its legal outcomes, institutional responses, and regulatory findings. Covers trials, settlements, Clery Act findings, financial and reputational impacts, and related commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fines for Clery Act Violations
rubrics_metrics.description: In November 2016, the U.S. Department of Education announced that it sought to fine Penn State nearly $2.4 million for violating the Clery Act. The violations include failing to alert the public about Sandusky's conduct and other campus dangers. Penn State officials have said that they will not appeal the fine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The announcement was accompanied by a list of specific findings (see Finding #1–#11) with proposed fines that together comprised the nearly $2.4 million total.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #1: Clery Act violations related to the Sandusky matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Clery Act violations related to the Sandusky matter (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly lists a proposed fine of $27,500 for Clery Act violations tied directly to the Sandusky matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #2: Lack of administrative capability
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of administrative capability as a result of the University's substantial failures to comply with the Clery Act and the Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act throughout the review period, including insufficient training, support, and resources to ensure compliance (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finding ties institutional administrative capacity and compliance systems to regulatory liability, noting training/support/resource shortfalls as the basis for the proposed fine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #3: Omitted/inadequate annual security and fire safety report policy statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Omitted and/or inadequate annual security report and annual fire safety report policy statements (proposed fine: $37,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed fine of $37,500 tied to deficiencies in required annual policy statements for security and fire safety reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #4: Failure to issue timely warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to issue timely warnings in accordance with federal regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This finding addresses the Clery Act obligation to provide timely public warnings about campus threats; no specific fine amount repeated here beyond the overall list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #5: Failure to properly classify and disclose crime statistics (2008–2011)
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to properly classify reported incidents and disclose crime statistics from 2008–2011 (proposed fine: $2,167,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the largest single proposed fine in the list ($2,167,500) and concerns misclassification and nondisclosure of crime data over multiple years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #6: Failure to establish adequate system for collecting crime statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to establish an adequate system for collecting crime statistics from all required sources (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses obligations to have systems in place to collect Clery-required statistics from all mandated sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #7: Failure to maintain accurate and complete daily crime log
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to maintain an accurate and complete daily crime log.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerns the operational requirement to keep a complete daily crime log as part of campus public safety transparency and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #8: Reporting discrepancies in published crime statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporting discrepancies in crime statistics published in the annual security report and those reported to the department's campus crime statistics database (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses inconsistency between different official crime-statistics disclosures; proposed fine specified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #9: Failure to publish and distribute annual security report
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to publish and distribute an annual security report in accordance with federal regulations (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifically targets the statutory requirement to produce and distribute the annual security report to the campus community and public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #10: Failure to notify prospective students and employees about report availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to notify prospective students and employees of the availability of the annual security report and annual fire safety report (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relates to the separate Clery/related obligation to inform prospective students/employees how to access required safety reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finding #11: Failure to comply with the Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Failure to comply with the Drug-Free Schools and Communities Act (proposed fine: $27,500).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flags noncompliance with drug-free campus statutory/regulatory obligations during the review period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settlement agreements requiring releases of third parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The settlement agreements required victims to release several organizations, and anyone connected to them, from lawsuits, including The Second Mile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contemporaneous commentary: an Indianapolis attorney representing sex-abuse victims said, 'That's not normal. Why would Penn State care about The Second Mile?' and said he had never encountered a defendant requesting a liability release for a separate organization. Alumni trustee Al Lord said, 'There's only one reason [for the release], and that was to protect ... members of the board who were involved at the Second Mile.' This entry highlights that settlements included broad third-party releases, which commentators found unusual and potentially protective of board members.
